caseno: First Appeal No. 128 of 1987 (FAT No. 359 of 1987).
lawyer:
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, with Mirza Hussain Haider, Advocates — For the Appellants 
Md Moksudur Rahman, with Md Fazlul Karim, Md Mazibar Rahman, Khondaker Modarresh Elahi and MA Mannad Mohan, Advocates — For the Respondents.
parties:
Shahani Bibi being dead her heirs: Mohammad Azim and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Nur Islam being dead his heirs: Doly Islam and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
The appellant as plaintiff on 11-12-1979 laid suit being Title Suit No. 893 of 1979 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which was, on transfer, re-numbered as Title Suit No. 574 of 1981 of the Third Court of Subordinate Judge in Dhaka. The subject matter of the suit appearing from the schedule to the plaint is 0.44 1/2 acres out of 0.89 acres of land on the northern portion of Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 under Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 within Mouza-Brahman Chiran under Police Station Tejgaon now Motijheel, District-Dhaka, State Acquisition Plots being 471 entire and 473 portion. 

 3. Averments made in the plaint are that Cadestral Survey Plot No. 112 measuring an area of 0.53 and Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 measuring an area of 0.89 acres of Mouza-Brahman Chiran, Police Station-Tejgaon, District-Dhaka belonged to Sk Mainuddin who sold the same orally to Chand Bepari for a consideration of Taka 75.00. Chand Bepari breathed his last leaving behind, among others, two sons, Sultan Hossain and Abed Sheikh, two daughters Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi. Saburannessa Bibi, Johara Bibi and some other heirs of Chand Bepari instituted a Suit being Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 for partition of the property including the aforesaid two plots left by Chand Bepari against Sultan Hossain and others in the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. In the said suit Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi got final decree and they took possession of the partitioned property through court. Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi sold their shares in several plots including the above stated two plots in favour of Kari Samiruddin Ahmed by a registered deed of conveyance dated 10-4-1922 who took over possession of the purchased land. Samiruddin, thereafter, on 30-5-1929 gifted half of the aforesaid plot Nos. 112 and 114 to Munshi Md Nowab Ali by a Deed of Gift dated 30-5-1929 and handed over the possession of the gifted property to the donee, Nowab Ali who subsequently transferred half of the Plot Nos. 112 and 114 to Sarama Sundari Guha by a registered Deed of Sale dated 5-1-1930. Sarama Sundari Guha got the northern portion of plot Nos. 112 and 114 by amicable partition among the co-sharers and, thereafter, sold the same to one Ramjan Ali by a registered Deed of Sale dated 8-12-1938. Ramjan Ali died leaving behind wife Faizun Nessa Bibi, 5 sons Abbas Ali, Ahmed Ali, Ansar, Abdur Razzak and Md Giasuddin and 2 daughters Amena Khatun and Sahara Khatun. 0.34 acres of land of plot No. 114 stood recorded in the name of Faizunnessa in State Acquisition Khatian Plot No. 473 and 0.37 acres of land of plot No. 114 was recorded in the name of Shamsuddin Mia who purchased from Asabuddin Mia and Abbasuddin Mia purchased from the heirs of Nowab Ali Mia and 0.18 acres of land of the said plot stood recorded in the name of the Province of East Pakistan in Khatian No. 1. 

 6. Averments made in the written statement filed by the defendant Nos. 1-9 are that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner. The suit is barred by limitation and principles of waiver and estoppel. The suit is bad mis-joinder and non-joinder of parties. The suit land is vague and indefinite. The plaintiff nor her predecessors had ever been in possession of the suit land and the suit is hit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The suit property belonged to Sk Mainuddin whose name had been correctly recorded in the Cadestral Survey Record of Right and Sk Mainuddin had been possessing the suit property by constructing but and cultivating the land and enjoying the usufructs therefrom. Sk Mainuddin died leaving behind 2 sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Hali. There had been no partition suit amongst the co-sharers of Chand Bepari and no possession was taken of plot Nos. 112 and 114 through court by the Decree Holders. The Deed of Gift in favour of Md Nowab Ali and the subsequent transfer by Nawab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha in respect of 2 decimals of land of plot No. 114 is bogus. Ramzan Ali by purchase from Sarams Sundari Guha also did not acquire any title nor possession in the suit property. The suit property was all along vacant nal land and most of the year the same remained under water. The suit property had been in possession of the defendants since their fore-father and the same stood recorded in their names in State Acquisition and Revisional Settlement Khatian. Rents had been paid with respect to suit property. The defendants are the heirs and successors of Abdul Halim and Abdus Sattar who were the sons of Sk Mainuddin. Plaintiff got no right, title and interest in the suit land and the title deeds of the plaintiff are false, collusive and without consideration. 

 8. Further pleading is, that Mainuddin Sk, who was also known as Mainuddin Kochoan, acquired the property of Cadestral Survey plot Nos. 114 and 112 from Sultan Hossain, son of Chand Bepari quite some time before the final publication of Cadestral Survey Record of Right and during the preparation of the said Record of Right, Mainuddin''''s name had been correctly recorded in CS Khatian No. 124. Out of the two Cadestral Survey plots, plot No. 112 with an area of 0.53 acres was the homestead of Mainuddin Sk and the other Cadestral Survey plot No. 114 having an area of 0.89 acres was nal land which always remained under deep water for several months during the rainy season and those remain unfit for cultivation for those months. Mainuddin Sk used to grow various kinds of vegetable during winter and dry season on the said plots. Mainuddin Sk having been in exclusive possession of the property of cadestral survey plot No. 114 died leaving behind two sons, Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim and the two brothers were in exclusive possession of the land of the said Cadestral Survey plot. Abdus Sattar died leaving behind his only son Abdul Mannan, defendant No. 6, Abdul Halim and Abdul Mannan were exercising acts of possession on the land of plot No. 114 by producing various kinds of vegetables after the recession of the rainy season. Abdul Halim died leaving behind one son Nurul Islam alias Nur Islam, defendant No. 1, three daughters Rezia Khatun, defendant No. 2, Tarana Begum defendant No. 3 and Hasina Begum defendant No. 5, and wife Begum Bibi defendant No. 4 and they used to exercise acts of possession on the land of plot No. 114 by growing paddy, various kinds of vegetable through Bargadars and hired labourers. The defendant Nos. 1-5, thereafter, having been in actual and physical possession of the land of Cadestral Survey plot No. 114 transferred land of the said plot in favour of the added defendant Nos. 10-17 for valuable consideration by several deeds of conveyance of different dates. The transferee defendant Nos. 10-17 are in actual possession of the land in respect of their respective shares in total denial of right, title and possession of all persons including the plaintiff. The particulars of the purchase of land by the defendant Nos. 10-17 have been given in a chart in the written statement. Clear assertion had been made by the defendants that the plaintiff never acquired any title to the suit property nor did she ever possess the land or any part thereof. 

 20. Defendant No. 11 is DW 3. He gave evidence on his behalf and also on behalf of defendant No. 10 who is his wife. He gave evidence in the same line as given by DWs 1 and 2. He and his wife also purchased 11/2 kathas of land from the suit property from Tarana Begum, the heir of Abdul Halim. He and his wife got their names mutated in the connected Record of Right and separate Khatians had been opened in their names. He and his wife got names mutated in the Municipality and Municipal Holding had been opened in their names and they paid Municipal Taxes and got Tax Receipts. He testified that the plaintiff did never exercise any acts of possession on the suit property. 

 c) No rebuttable evidence could be adduced by the plaintiff to show that Cadestral Survey Khatian was wrongly prepared which, in fact, got presumptive value. 

 e) From the certified copy of the sale deed by Munshi Nowab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha it appeared that Nowab Ali sold 2 decimals of land of CS plot No. 124 under khatian No. 124 and on close scrutiny it appeared that CS plot No. 124 was made as 114 by over writing with a view to tally the same with the suit plot No. 114. From Exhibit-6 it appeared that Sarama Sundari Guha sold 0.44½ acres of land of CS plot No. 114 whereas it appeared from the schedule No. 6 of Exhibit 5 that Sarama Sundari Guha purchased only 0.02 decimals of land of CS plot No. 124 and, thus, Sarama Sundari Guha could not sell 0.44½ acres of land to Ramjan Al and the legal heirs of Ramjan Ali could not transfer. 0.331/2 acres of land to the plaintiff and 0.13 acres of land to Sona Mia by Exhibits 7 and 8 respectively. 

 f) Exhibit 10 is the certified copy of Mutated Khatian in favour of the plaintiff for 0.101/2 acres of land but no order of the Mutation Case was filed to show whether the defendant Nos. 1-9 who are legal heirs of the CS recorded owner Sk Mainuddin were parties in that proceeding. 

 iii) The presumption attached to the SC Record of Right in the name of Mainuddin Kochwan had been successfully rebutted by the plaintiff and Decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 is a rebuttable piece of evidence and the court fell into an error in holding that no rebuttable evidence could be adduced by the plaintiff to show that CS Khatian was wrongly prepared and the CS Khatian got a presumptive value. 

 33. In approaching the appeal and before examination of the merit of the contentions it needs taking notice that in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916, the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hussain was the son of Chand Bepari who was the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs of the stated suit including plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 Saburennessa Bibi and Johra Bibi who are the predecessor-in-interest of the present plaintiff. The defendant Nos. 2-30 including the defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan were transferees from defendant No. 1 Sultan Hussain. Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim were the two sons of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan and Abdul Halim is the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos. 1-5. The defendant Nos. 10-17 are transferees from defendant Nos. 1-5. It is also to be borne in mind that the subject matter of the present suit is Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 corresponding to State Acquisition Plot No. 471 and portion of plot No. 473 and the plaintiff as the transferee by way of two Sale Deeds claims acquisition of title on the suit property on the basis of a Decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 of the Fifth Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on schedule Ka, Uma and Cha-Tha (ত) property specifically schedule property as Cha and Tha (ত) and the said schedule properties were described by boundary alone in the plaint. 

 40. Another contention has been also advanced from the side of the plaintiff-appellant that the defendant No. 6 of the present suit land a Suit being Title Suit No. 261 of 1982 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka wherein the present plaintiff was defendant No. 8 and the defendant No. 6 admitted that the schedule Cha and Tha (5) land of Exhibit 1 are the land of Suit Khatian No. 124. It appears that the said suit was withdrawn on the question of formal defect in the plaint. In the said Title Suit No. 261 of 1982 all the defendants of the present suit specially the defendant Nos. 10-17 were not parties. The plaintiff of the suit could not be examined nor the averments made in the plaint of the suit could be confronted to the plaintiff as because in the event of withdrawal of the suit there was no scope left for the said plaintiff to have been examined in the court not to speak of any confrontation with respect to the plaint of that suit. Law is settled that the previous statement of any person cannot be taken into consideration if that person is not examined as witness in the court and the said statement not confronted with the previous statement as enshrined in section 145 of the Evidence Act. This contention, thus, stands rejected as being without any merit. 

 41. From the above it, thus, manifests that the plaintiff signally failed to discharge the burden that lay on her or, in other words, failed to prove that the property detailed in the schedule including schedule Cha and Tha (ত) property of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 attracted Cadestral Survey Plot No. 144 of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 which is the suit property of the present suit. Unless the plaintiff proves that the property stated in the schedule of the previous suit attracted the present suit plot (Cadestral Survey Suit Plot No. 124), the plaintiff cannot at all claim title on the present suit property and her title cannot be also declared thereon. The learned Trial Judge noticed and considered this vital aspect of the case and arrived at a correct decision. We are in total agreement with the said adjudication of the matter. 

 54. Turning now to the question whether the plaintiff, on the basis of her two title deeds, Exhibit 7 and 9, and other supporting evidences, can be said to have acquired title on the suit property and whether she could prove her possession thereon. It appears that the Decree-Holders, Saburennessa Bibi and Johara Bibi by Exhibit 3 transferred the suit property in favour of Kari Samsuddin from schedule No. 6 of the said deed and they transferred the land of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 123 and not the land of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124. PW 1, the son of the plaintiff in his evidence stated that Saburennessa and Johara Bibi sold the land of plot Nos. 112 and 114 of Khatian No. 123. He also testified that the Khatian No. 123 had been wrongly stated in the said Exhibit 3. It transpires, further, from Exhibit 4, the Deed of Gift by Kari Shamsuddin in favour of Munshi Nowab Ali, the said Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 123 appeared. Exhibit 5 is the Sale deed by Munshi Nowab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha. From Exhibit 5 it manifests that Munshi Nowab Ali transferred 0.02 acres of land of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124. Vehement argument had been put forward from the side of the defendant-respondents that in Exhibit 5, CS Plot No. 124 had been made 114 by interpolation. The plaintiff-appellant filed an Index showing the plot numbers transferred in the Sale deed No. 118 which is Exhibit 5. Though the Index had not been admitted into evidence and marked as Exhibit but this court feels inclined in taking judicial notice of the said Index. On a careful perusal of the said Index it appears that there is mention of deed No. 118. In Exhibit 5, the Sale deed by Nowab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha bore Deed No. 118 and plot Nos. 112 and 114 appear there. So, it is difficult to accept the contention raised from the side of defendant-respondents that Cadestral Survey Plot No. 124 had been made plot No. 114 by interpolation. 

 56. Exhibit 10 is the certified copy of the Mutated Khatian in the name of Faizunnessa, the wife of Ramjan Ali with respect to 0.34 acres of land. Exhibit 12 is the corrected Record of Right standing in the name of the plaintiff on the basis of an order of the Revenue Officer dated 30-4-1972. Exhibit F is the objection laid by Nurul Islam and others, the heirs of Abdul Halim who are defendant Nos. 1-5 raising objection against the Record of Right prepared in the name of Faizunnessa recording her name in the Record of Right. Exhibit 9 is the Report of Badar Amin who on holding Local Inspection found objector Nurul Islam and others in possession of the land. Exhibit F (1) is the Order dated 27-10-1978 passed by the Revenue Officer allowing the objection. In the said order the name of Faizunnessa was ordered to be struck off and there was further order for correcting the record in the name of the objectors, Nurul Islam and others. Exhibit ''''H'''' is the corrected Record of Right standing in the named of Nurul Islam and others. In the event of the striking off the name of Faizunnessa from the Record of Right and recording the names of Nurul Islam and others in the Record of Right by the order of the Revenue Officer dated 27-10-1978, the Record of Right in the name of the plaintiff fell to ground as because the plaintiff was to rise and fall with Faizunnessa. Exhibit 11 is the certified copy of the order dated 7-11-1970 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 294 of 1969 of the First Court of Munsiff, Dhaka allowing the case ex parte wherein the Record of Right was ordered to be prepared in the name of the plaintiff with respect to 0.10½ acres of land. It appears that only the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka was made opposite party in the Miscellaneous Case and the heirs of Mainuddin Sheikh alias Kochwan, the defendant Nos. 1-9 were not made opposite parties. Therefore, the order passed in the Miscellaneous Case for recording the name of the plaintiff without impleading the defendant Nos. 1-9 who are the heirs of Mainuddin Sheikh alias Kochwan cannot be binding upon them and the said order is of no avail to the defendant Nos. 1-9 and also to the defendant Nos. 10-17 who are the transferees from them. Exhibit 13 is a private Rent Receipt allegedly granted in favour of Ramjan Ali by the alleged Naib of the alleged Landlord. Exhibit 13(a), 14(a) and 14(b) are Government Rent Receipts showing payment of rent. But it is to be remembered that mere mutation and payment of rents do not confer any title on any person. 

 57. Exhibit A is the certified copy of the Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 standing in the name of Mainuddin Sheikh alias Kochwan. Exhibit B-B(2), MNRS W-W(1) are the Deeds of Conveyance executed by defendant Nos. 1-5, the heirs of Abdul Halim in favour of the defendant Nos.10-17. Exhibit C, K, O, T and Y are certified copies of the Record of Rights (Mutated Khatian) recording the names of the defendant Nos. 10-17 with respect to the suit property. Exhibits D-D(1), L, P, U and Y are the Rent Receipts evidencing payment of rents to the Revenue authority with respect to the suit property. Exhibits E, Q-Q(2), V-V(2) and Z-Z(1) are Dhaka Municipal Corporation Tax Receipts manifesting payment of Taxes to Dhaka Municipal Corporation for the suit property by the defendant Nos. 10-17. 

 63. Cadastral Survey Record of Right is the oldest Record of Right in our country. Onus of proving that Cadestral Survey Record of Right is wrong is on the person who alleges it. The plaintiff-appellant challenged the correctness of the Cadestral Survey Record of Right and so onus is definitely upon the plaintiff to show that entry in the Record of Right as prepared under section 103 (B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is wrong. In Aminuddin Biswas vs Miajan Biswas, 12 DLR 103 it has been held: The presumption of correctness as available on the strength of section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act has got to be rebutted by the person who alleges it : In this context it needs be stated that where a person relies upon the entry in the Record of Right for the basis of his title he is not required to show the basis of the entry in the Record of Right. It is also to be noted that the presumption attached to the Cadestral Record of Right prepared under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is not rebutted on the reason that there is no evidence for the basis of the entry. In Alauddin Munshi and others vs Mainuddin Talukder and others, 14 DLR 725 it has been posited: Merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of right, the presumption is not rebutted in view of the provision of the Bengal Tenancy Act and also the procedure laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the officer concerned while preparing the final records of rights. There must be further evidence to show that the evidences are incorrect : In Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Karia and others, 30 DLR (SC) 81, the presumption of the correctness of an entry in the Record of Right has been considered. It has been laid down by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court that according to section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act every entry in the Record of Right finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. It had already been pointed out that in the plaint of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 in paragraph 4 there is clear averment that the defendant No.1 Sultan Hossain and the defendants 2-30 who are the transferees from defendant No.1 were in possession of the entire suit property detailed in the schedule of the said suit. The learned Advocate Commissioner found Abdus Sattar in possession of Schedule Cha and Tha (3) land and in the Field Book he noted the possession of Abdus Sattar on the said Cha and Tha (3) land. There is no evidence that the decree of partition Suit had been executed on evicting the defendants especially the heirs of defendant No. 21, Abdus Sattar and the Decree-Holder plaintiffs specially plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 of the said suit, Saburennessa and Johara Bibi got into possession of the decreed land. The Cadestral Survey Record of Right was finally published in the district of Dhaka round about the year 1929, perhaps before the amendment of Bengal Tenancy Act in 1929. The plaintiff has not adduced any evidence at all what was the state of possession of the suit land at the time of preparation of Cadestral Survey Record of Right. The decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 having not been executed at all, the said decree cannot be said to be a rebuttable piece of evidence rebutting the presumption of the correctness of the Cadestral Survey Record of Right standing in the name of Mainuddin Sheikh alias Mainuddin Kochwan. The presumption of the correctness of the entry in the Cadestral Survey Record of Right does not appear to have been rebutted by the plaintiff-appellant. The learned trial Judge on consideration of the legal evidences and materials on record recorded the finding that no rebuttable evidence could be adduced by the plaintiff to show that CS Khatian was wrongly prepared which, in fact, got presumptive value. No exception can be taken to the said decision arrived at by the trial Judge.
